paragraphs: I would fulfill the purpose of this book only imperfectly if I showed which opinions and feelings the principle of equality suggests, and then closed without pointing out their general influence on how human societies are governed. To do this I will often have to go back over ground already covered. I trust the reader will still follow me down paths he already knows, since they may lead to some new truth.

The principle of equality makes men independent of one another. It gives them the habit and the taste of following only their own will in their private actions. They enjoy this complete independence all the time, toward their equals and in the dealings of private life. It inclines them to regard every authority with jealousy, and it soon puts the idea and love of political freedom into their heads. Men who live in such times lean naturally toward free institutions. Pick any one of them at random and search, if you can, his most deeply rooted instincts. Of all governments, you will find, the one he will most quickly imagine and most highly prize is the one whose head he has elected himself and whose administration he can control. Of all the political effects of equality of conditions, this love of independence is the first to strike the observer and to alarm the timid. Their alarm is not wholly misplaced, either, because anarchy looks more formidable in democratic countries than elsewhere. Citizens have no direct influence on one another. If the supreme power of the nation fails, the power that kept each of them in his place, disorder would seem bound to reach its peak at once. Every man would go off in a different direction, and the fabric of society would immediately fall to pieces.

Nonetheless I am convinced that anarchy is the least of the evils democratic ages have to fear, not the chief one. The principle of equality produces two tendencies. One carries men straight to independence and can drive them suddenly into anarchy. The other takes them to servitude along a longer, more hidden, but surer road. Nations easily notice the first tendency and are ready to resist it. The second sweeps them along without their seeing where it ends, and that is why it matters so much to point it out. As for me, I do not blame the principle of equality for making men hard to govern. That very quality is what I mainly approve of in it. I admire how it plants in the mind and heart of man a dim notion and an instinctive love of political independence, and so prepares the cure for the evil it causes. For this reason I am attached to it.
